title: Clap, Clap, Boom!
blurb: Mumble has no drum, but Mama Bear says his drum is always with him: clap, clap, boom! When Mumble rushes and muddles it up, he stops, breathes, listens and finds the rhythm.

pages.text: The forest morning was all a-twitter. A sparrow sang: cheep cheep! Little bear Mumble sighed. “I haven't got a drum!” Mama Bear smiled. “Your drum is always with you!”

anne.say: Your drum is always with you!

pages.ask: Where do you think Mumble's drum could be?

pages.text: Mama Bear clapped her paws: clap, clap! She stamped her foot: boom! “There's your drum!” Mumble tried fast, fast: boom, clap, boom! All in a muddle! Mumble got cross. His cheeks went hot.

mirmir.say: Boom, clap, boom! It's not working!

pages.ask: What happens in your body when you get cross?

pages.text: “Stop, take a breath,” said Mama Bear. Mumble breathed in, and let it out: fwooo. They laid out leaves and a stone in a row. Clap, clap, boom, clap, clap… What comes next?

anne.say: Stop, take a breath. Listen first.

predict.q: What comes next: a leaf or a stone?
predict.res: Come on, let's play it and hear!

pages.hint: Touch the leaves and the stone!
pages.ask: How did you know? Come on, let's say it out loud together: clap, clap, boom, clap, clap...

pages.text: Next came the stone: boom! Now Mumble played slowly. Leaf clap, leaf clap, stone boom! Mumble smiled: “I did it!”

mirmir.say: Clap, clap, boom! I did it!

anne.say: You played slowly, you listened; there it is!

mech.done: Clap, clap, boom! Mumble did it!

pages.hint: Touch them in order: clap, clap, boom!
pages.ask: Come on, you play too: clap, clap, boom! Which made the stronger sound, your hands or your feet?

pages.text: Wiggle the squirrel came running. “Let me play too!” They took turns. Wiggle clap! Mumble clap! Mama Bear boom!

mech.done: Clap, clap, boom! What a lovely song!

pages.ask: Who said clap, and who said boom? Which one would you like to play with your friend?

pages.text: Clap, clap, boom! Clap, clap, boom! The whole forest danced. Mumble patted his tummy: boom! “My drum was with me all along!”

mirmir.say: My drum was with me all along!

pages.ask: What sounds can you make with your hands and feet?

kazanim: MÇB3 Musical Playing (unverified) · “Playing the sounds they hear”: Plays the clap-clap-boom rhythm from the story by clapping hands and stamping feet, using the body as an instrument.
MDB.1 · “Listening to a variety of musical works”: Listens carefully to a rhythm before playing it; tells the forest sounds (cheep cheep, clap, boom) apart from each other.
HSAB.6 · “Performing movement patterns in harmony with a partner/group”: Builds a shared rhythm by doing clap-clap-boom in turns with friends.
SDB1.2 Self-Regulation · When he rushes and muddles it up, he stops, breathes and listens first; notices how anger feels in the body (cheeks go hot).
Value · D7 Aesthetics: Enjoys creating a beautiful rhythm with sounds from his own body.
once: Show the cover: ask “Mumble has no instrument in his hands. How can he make music?”
Clap your hands together (clap) and stamp your foot on the floor (boom). Which sound is stronger?
Show a few leaves and a stone: “Today a leaf will mean clap, and a stone will mean boom.”
sirasi: When Mama Bear plays, do clap, clap, boom too; when Mumble muddles it up, smile together, but also give his anger a name.
On the “Stop, take a breath” page, all breathe in through your nose together and let it out slowly with a “fwooo”.
On the prediction page, wait for the child's answer; ask “Why did you think that?” Repeating the rhythm out loud makes the answer easier to find.
On the page where Wiggle arrives, play in turns with the children: one person clap, one person clap, one person boom.
At 36–48 months, start with AB (clap, boom, clap, boom); once the child is comfortable, move to AAB (clap, clap, boom).
sonra: Wrap up the story with the picture-ordering game: all in a muddle → playing with leaves and a stone → all together.
Ask “What did Mumble do when he got cross? Did it work?” (he stopped, took a breath, listened first). Pat your tummy, pat pat: “Where was Mumble's drum?”
Try new patterns: first AB (clap, boom, clap, boom), then AAB (clap, clap, boom) once the child is comfortable. Let the children say what comes next.
Ask the children to find their own body sounds: pat pat on the knees, tap tap on the chest, finger snaps.

sinif.materyal: Leaves cut from green card, flat stones cut from grey card (or real big leaves), tape to stick them to the floor
adim: Lay out leaf, leaf, stone, leaf, leaf, stone on the floor. On a leaf you clap your hands (clap), on a stone you stamp your foot (boom).
The children take turns walking from the start of the row, playing the sound as they step on each card; the group says it all together: clap, clap, boom!
Then leave the end of the row empty: “What comes next?” The child puts down the right card and plays it.
In the reflection circle, ask: “What happened when you rushed? How did it feel to play slowly?”

evSoru: How did Mumble feel when he muddled up the rhythm? What did he do next?
What sounds can you make with your hands and feet?

evEtk.d: In the kitchen or living room, lay out two towels (clap) and a cushion (boom). Let your child play clap, clap, boom as they walk over the row. Then you set up the order and they continue it; at the end, let them make up their own rhythm and you copy it.

guide.aileNotu: Today we read “Clap, Clap, Boom!” Mumble had no drum; Mama Bear showed him that his body is an instrument too. When Mumble rushed and muddled it up, he stopped, took a breath and listened first. At home you can play clap, clap, boom by clapping hands and stamping feet, and keep the pattern going together; stopping to take a breath when you rush is part of the game too.
